MINUTES
  PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING
  MONDAY, OCTOBER 7, 2024

A regular meeting of the Planning Commission of the City of Rolling Hills Estates was called to
order by CHAIR MEDAWAR at 7:00 p.m. in the City Hall Council Chamber.

2.  SALUTE TO THE FLAG

COMMISSIONER ROMANELLI led those assembled in the Pledge of Allegiance.

3.  ROLL CALL

  Commissioners Present:  Medawar, Olson, Nicklas, Repp-Loadsman, Romanelli,
  Schachter, Yoo

  City Staff Present:  Jeannie Naughton, Community Development Director
  Whitney Berry, Senior Planner
  Carol Corea, Administrative Analyst

  Also Present:  Steve McEwen, Assistant City Attorney

4.  APPROVAL OF MINUTES

A.  APPROVAL OF PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING MINUTES, SEPTEMBER 3, 2024

COMMISSIONER SCHACHTER, seconded by VICE CHAIR OLSON to,

  APPROVE THE PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING MINUTES OF SEPTEMBER 3,
  2024.

There being no objection, CHAIR MEDAWAR so ordered.

5.  AUDIENCE ITEMS

NONE

6.  CONSENT CALENDAR

NONE

7.  BUSINESS ITEMS

A.  PLANNING APPLICATION NO. PA-240315; ADDRESS: 25 Empty Saddle Lane, Rolling
  Hills Estates, CA 90274; APPLICANT: Quetzal Silver, Quicksilver Drafting; A request for
  a Neighborhood Compatibility Determination (NC-240316) for a new 140 ft. CMU block
  retaining wall along the north side property line and a Grading Permit (G-240317) for the
  import of 160 cubic yards of earth material to fill a slope with a vertical height of more than
  three feet at its deepest point.

Assistant Planner Kawagoe provided a presentation summarizing the staff report for Planning
Application No. PA-240315. Staff received two comment letters from the neighbor at 21 Empty
Saddle Lane, one of which was attached to the staff report and the second provided as a
supplemental correspondence and emailed to the Planning Commission for review on the day of
the meeting. The neighbor expressed concerns with the wall that separates the two properties
and the effect it will have on his property; he requested a soils test, structural and drainage plans,
and stated that he does not believe the project should be exempt from CEQA. Assistant Planner
Kawagoe confirmed that this project is categorically exempt from CEQA since it is for the
construction of a small structure for a single-family residence. The soils testing, structural and
drainage plans, will be addressed during the building permit process. The neighbor also raised
concerns with the design of the wall since it will not match the wall surrounding his front yard
entryway as the wall is finished with stucco, and requested that this item be continued until these
issues have been addressed. Assistant Planner Kawagoe stated that staff does not recommend

 PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 7, 2024
  1
 this action since the applicant has met the requirements of the municipal code.

Assistant Planner Kawagoe stated that staff recommends that the Planning Commission approve
Planning Application No. PA-240315 subject to the conditions outlined in the staff report.

COMMISSIONER SCHACHTER asked why the applicant is proposing this project. Assistant
Planner Kawagoe stated that the applicant would like to recapture as much of the year yard as
possible since they have plans to build a pool.

VICE CHAIR OLSON asked if staff addressed the concerns of the first letter received by the
neighbor. Assistant Planner Kawagoe stated that she met with the neighbor, the project designer
and contractor to discuss the scope of the project.

COMMISSIONER NICKLAS asked if the project complies with CEQA. Assistant Planner
Kawagoe stated that it does since they are proposing to build a small structure for a single-family
residence and the concern with infill will be addressed during the building permitting process.

VICE CHAIR OLSON asked if a grading plan will be required. Assistant Planner Kawagoe stated
that it will, additionally a structural and drainage plan will also be required.

VICE CHAIR OLSON asked if the fill will be compacted under observation. Assistant Planner
Kawagoe stated that she believes it will.

George Lopez, Project Contractor, stated that the applicant has already stated that the wall will
be finished with stucco and the concern of the neighbor in regard to this will not be an issue.

Quetzal Silver, Project Designer, stated that he is willing to modify the plans to include the stucco
and this will not be an issue.

COMMISSIONER ROMANELLI stated that he reviewed the plans and asked about pylons or
caissons for the project. Mr. Silver stated that a soils test will be required by building and safety
and at that time they will determine what will be required; he stated that in his experience pylons
or caissons will not be required for this type of project and will require a standard 12-inch footing.

COMMISSIONER NICKLAS made a motion, seconded by COMMISSIONER SCHACHTER to,

  APPROVE PLANNING APPLICATION NO. PA-240315  (SUBJECT  TO  THE
  CONDITIONS OUTLINED IN THE STAFF REPORT).

AYES: MEDAWAR, OLSON, NICKLAS, REPP-LOADSMAN, ROMANELLI, SCHACHTER, YOO
NOES:
ABSENT:
ABSTAIN:

Director Naughton stated that the Planning Commission has approved Planning Application No.
PA-240315. There is a 20-day appeal period by which any member of the public or the City
Council by its own motion may appeal this decision.

8.  PUBLIC HEARINGS

A.  PLANNING APPLICATION NO. PA-240062; ADDRESS: 4665 Browndeer Lane, Rolling
  Hills Estates, CA 90274; APPLICANT: Curtis Fortier; A request for approval of a
  Neighborhood Compatibility Determination (NC-240064) for a 317 SF second-story
  addition, 172 SF front yard addition, and 154 SF first floor, rear yard addition with 257 SF
  covered patio to an existing two-story single-story resident. Additional request for approval
  include a Minor Deviation (MD-240063) to encroach into a required front yard that does
  not project closer to the front property line than the forwardmost building line, and a
  Variance (V-240065) to exceed the height to setback ratio to continue to build along
  existing building lines that encroach into the nonconforming west side yard.

Assistant Planner Kawagoe provided a presentation summarizing the staff report for Planning
Application No. PA-240062.

Assistant Planner Kawagoe stated that staff recommends that the Planning Commission open
the public hearing, take public testimony, discuss the issues, close the public hearing, and adopt
Resolution No. PA-240062.

COMMISSIONER NICKLAS asked if the change in setback is in the front and the rear of the
property. Assistant Planner Kawagoe confirmed that the change is in the front and the rear.

 PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 7, 2024
  2
 COMMISSIONER YOO asked if any comments were received from the neighbors. Assistant
Planner Kawagoe stated that staff did not receive any comments for this project.

COMMISSIONER MEDAWAR disclosed that he has a property up the street from this property in
the neighboring city.

VICE CHAIR OLSON made a motion, seconded by COMMISSIONER YOO to,

  OPEN THE PUBLIC HEARING

There being no objection, CHAIR MEDAWAR so ordered.

Janelle Doose, Property Owner, stated that they are trying to expand the house, while keeping
with the architectural design of the house. She stated that a survey was done, and it showed that
one of the fences between the neighbor is in the wrong location and they have a little room to
expand; however, it is only a matter of inches and they still need the variance.

In response to a question by CHAIR MEDAWAR, Ms. Doose stated that the neighbor and her
have no concern with the current location of the fence.

CHAIR MEDAWAR made a motion, seconded by COMMISSIONER YOO to,

  CLOSE THE PUBLIC HEARING

There being no objection, CHAIR MEDAWAR so ordered.

COMMISSIONER SCHACHTER made a motion, seconded by COMMISSIONER YOO to,

  APPROVE PLANNING APPLICATION NO. PA-240062 ADOPTING RESOLUTION NO.
  240062.

 Ayes: MEDAWAR, OLSON, NICKLAS, SCHACHTER, REPP-LOADSMAN, ROMANELLI, YOO
 Noes:
 Absent:
 Abstain:

Director Naughton stated that the Planning Commission has adopted Resolution No. PA-240062,
approving Planning Application No. PA-240062. There is a 20-day appeal period by which any
member of the public or the City Council by its own motion may appeal this decision.

B.  PLANNING APPLICATION NO. PA-230516; ADDRESS: 27525 NORRIS CENTER
  DRIVE, ROLLING HILLS ESTATES; APPLICANT: RYAN ASH ON BEHALF OF VESTAR;
  DESCRIPTION: Consideration of a Precise Plan of Design, a Commercial District Mixed-
  Use Development Permit, and a Development Agreement for a 90-unit apartment project
  on a 2-acre site in the Peninsula Shopping Center.

Senior Planner Berry presented Planning Application No. PA-230516 summarizing the staff
report. This was a continuation of the public hearing for this project from the August 3rd Planning
Commission meeting. Senior Planner Whitney stated that there were a number of concerns and
requests for additional information raised by the Planning Commission. The Planning Commission
expressed a concern that the proposed 20-year term deed restriction for the affordable units
compared to the 55-year term required for low-income rental units under the State density bonus
law. The Planning Commission requested a minimum 30-year term in order to provide a better
community benefit balance. The applicant has agreed to extend the term to 35 years.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the Planning Commission expressed concerns about the value
to the community of the public parking spaces and the use of those public spaces and explained
that public parking on private property within the commercial district is an identified community
amenity on the Council approval list of amenities and benefits associated with the City’s bonus
level development program. As a condition of approval, the applicant will be required to prepare
a parking management agreement with the city that further details how the public parking will be
set aside for the community. These spaces will also be used for city-sponsored events such as
the Holiday Parade and Street Fair, community organizations, and other events that may require
temporary reservation of these spaces. Access to and from the parking spaces will be provided
via pathways that are required to be ADA compliant and in line with the California Building Code.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the Planning Commission requested additional information about
the existing parking variance and explained that the Peninsula Shopping Center has
approximately 290,143 feet of leasable retail space and 1124 parking spaces, which results in a

 PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 7, 2024
  3
 parking ratio of 1 space to 258 square feet. This was confirmed by Vestar after an on-site parking
count. The Peninsula Shopping Center is in compliance with its parking variance that was granted
by the Planning Commission in 2014 and when the lot line adjustment was performed in 2019,
which allows for space per 269 square feet of leasable area.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the Planning Commission expressed concerns about the security
and use of the private parking spaces and explained that the project proposes a residential access
gate to secure the residential parking on the second level, and as a condition of approval for this
project, the applicant will be required to prepare a parking management agreement further
detailing the use and management of the private stalls. In addition, there was concern expressed
about the proximity of certain residential spaces to the garage wall located on aisles with dead
end conditions. The applicant has revised the site plan to include labels showing the proposed
distances for those dead-end aisle conditions, which range from three to eight feet.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the Planning Commission expressed a concern about the value
to the community of the proposed public plaza. The proposed public plaza is a contributing
amenity that the City Council considered in their preliminary determination in March, that the
proposal met the proposed density and benefit balance to qualify the project to be analyzed for
the purposes of CEQA.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the Planning Commission requested that staff include conditions
of approval requiring will serve letters from all utility providers prior to issuance of the building
permits and the proposed Planning Commission resolution, which has been revised.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the Planning Commission also inquired about the review process
for street trees proposed by the project along the public right of way. The Landscape Plan shows
many trees across the site with three street trees on the public right of way along Norris Drive. As
a condition of approval for this project, the applicant will be required to work with city staff to
present that plan to the Park and Activities Commission including information about the tree
species and other landscape improvements proposed for that right of way.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the Planning Commission expressed some concerns about
future traffic in the area on account of future developments within the commercial district. There
was a non-CEQA supplemental transportation assessment conducted for the project which
identified the effects of the proposed project on the surrounding transportation system in
accordance with the City's guidelines. The analysis did not recommend any intersection
improvements as a Condition of approval for this project and the city's traffic engineer concurred
with that conclusion.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the last item of concern from the Planning Commission was
about certain sections of the development agreement having to do with transfer agreements and
encumbrances. Staff consulted with the City Attorney's office, who advised that the development
agreement would in fact be recorded against the property so that any purchases of the property
will be on notice of the rights and obligations of the agreement. Sometimes an owner may not sell
the property, but instead bring in an investor or another party to develop a part of the project while
the owner remains on the title; Section 8.2 of the development agreement addresses such a
situation.

Senior Planner Berry stated that the project was reviewed in accordance with CEQA and the State
CEQA guidelines and an Addendum to the City’s 2040 General Plan EIR was prepared for the
project. There are no conditions or circumstances warranting greater subsequent or supplemental
review in this case and the proposed project would not result in substantial changes requiring
major revisions to the previous EIR.

Senior Planner Berry stated that following tonight’s decision or determination by the Planning
Commission, staff plan to bring their recommendation to the Council at its October 22nd meeting.
Staff received one comment letter, which came in the same day as the meeting and was
forwarded to the Planning Commission by email for review. This letter came from the California
Housing Defense Fund in support of the project.

Senior Planner Berry stated that staff recommends that the Planning Commission open the public
hearing, receive public testimony, discuss the issues, close the public hearing, and adopt
Resolution No. PA-230516 recommending the City Council approve a Commercial District Mixed-
Use Development permit, approve a Precise Plan of Design, adopt Ordinance No. 750 to enter
into a Development Agreement with the applicant and adopt the addendum to the 2040 General
Plan EIR.

CHAIR MEDAWAR asked for clarification on the process for this project given that this is the first
project that he recalls received the City Council’s approval prior to coming before the Planning

 PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 7, 2024
  4
 Commission. Director Naughton stated that there was a new process that was created with the
City’s bonus level development program, which requires that the City Council make a preliminary
determination of whether or not the attributes included in the proposed project meets the threshold
for bonus level development. The City Council felt that the amenities being proposed met the
threshold for bonus level development and that the applicants could go ahead and proceed with
CEQA. It was not approval of the project but rather that it met the threshold and could move
forward with the process.

COMMISSIONER ROMANELLI stated that at the last meeting there were questions about
infrastructure compatibility and stated that the resolution captured all except telecommunications
upgrades and solid waste removal. He also stated that the resolution includes that “the cost for
the water and sewer infrastructure will be borne by the applicant”, but this statement is not
included for all the utilities. Director Naughton stated that staff can add language to clarify this,
and that typically, when will-serve letters are required, and an upgrade or infrastructure is needed,
the letter will condition this action, and the cost will be borne by the applicant.

In response to a question by COMMISSIONER NICKLAS, Senior Planner Berry stated that per
the appraisal the valuation for the 85 public parking spaces $4.428M, the public plaza $773,400
and the nine affordable units $3,109,400. The valuation for the affordable units is detailed in the
appraisal report. The value to the City of the affordable units is that there will now be nine
affordable units to residents of the community who may need such housing.

CHAIR MEDAWAR stated that the value of each unit is $345K/unit, which is a lower value of
equivalent units.

COMMISSIONER NICKLAS provided a sample calculation stating that the developer will recoup
their investment in four years and in ten years they will make $12.6M and in twenty years $25.2M.
He also stated that the 85 parking spots may be used by the public but will most likely be used by
the residents. He stated that he is concerned with the true value to the City, relative to the
investment of the developer.

VICE CHAIR OLSON stated that the development agreement states that the reserve parking
spaces can be used by patrons of the Peninsula Shopping Center when not in use for and agreed
upon use. He questioned the value of these spaces to the City.

VICE CHAIR OLSON asked if the preliminary approval of the City Council included the community
amenities as presented. Director Naughton stated that it did. The project was not approved, the
City Council’s preliminary decision just said that the proposed project meets the threshold for
granting bonus level development. The threshold outlined in the code is 25% of the fair market
cost; this proposal is at 73%.

In response to a question by VICE CHAIR OLSON, Director Naughton stated that parking on
private property is not allowed to be utilized by the public and further explained why this was
added to the list of amenities that can be used by a developer. She further provided an explanation
for creating the Bonus Level Development Program in the city.

VICE CHAIR OLSON questioned if a developer offered the City $2M dollars to add to the General
Fund to use how the City deems fit, would the City invest in building a parking structure. He stated
that he cannot find anyone who would support this idea.

COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN stated that she appreciates the Director’s comments in
terms of the City Council providing feedback and direction; however, the City Council has referred
this project to the Planning Commission to review the details of the project and policy decisions
through the general plan. She stated that she does not believe that the Planning Commission is
constrained by what the City Council preliminarily approved.

COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN stated that if the developer were to use the State Density
Bonus Law, then the City would get affordable housing at a 55-year term, which is a significant
community benefit.

COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN stated that providing public parking does provide a
community benefit to the city. She added that affordable housing going from a 20-year tern to a
35-year term is much better given that the developer is willing to give other concessions and a
longstanding relationship with the City.

COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN stated that the letter received from the California Housing
Defense Fund (CalHDF) has the tone that the City is obligated to approve the project because of
affordability. However, being that given that the City has a subjective review and the requirement
for a development agreement, the City does have discretion and is not bound by any obligation

 PLANNING COMMISSION MEETING
 MINUTES, OCTOBER 7, 2024
  5
 as suggested in the CalHDF letter. Assistant City Attorney McEwen agreed and stated that the
City does have discretion and does not agree with the legal contentions set forth in the letter from
CalHDF.

COMMISSIONER SCHACHTER stated that he agrees with the other commissioners that the
parking will not be used by the public and will be used by the residents, which affects the valuation.
He also stated that if the public parking was outdoors, the valuation would not be $4.4M. He stated
that he does not see the community benefit of this covered public parking structure, which will not
be used by the public most of the time.

COMMISSIONER YOO stated that he agrees with the commissioners. He expressed his concern
with the part of the community benefit that includes the value of the affordable units at $3.1M and
asked if a developer would still receive a 50% density bonus if they did not provide the public
parking and instead increased the affordable housing units from nine to twenty. His concern is
that he does not want to see a situation where a developer will agree to build more affordable
units in order to receive a 50% density bonus. He also stated that he does not agree with the
valuation of the public parking spaces. Director Naughton stated that Resolution No. 2531, lists
the twelve community benefits that the City Council identified to qualify for the Density Bonus
Program. She explained that if any of the benefits were chosen, the developer would need to
provide an independent appraisal report for the cost of the amenities and the City Council has
discretion to make the preliminary determination to qualify for the density level bonus.

COMMISSIONER YOO stated that he is not comfortable agreeing with the value of the community
benefit.

COMMISSIONER SCHACHTER stated that the problem with the ordinance is that the applicant
provides the appraisal report and there is no evidence of what it is truly worth.

COMMISSIONER YOO stated that the affordable units are owned and controlled by the developer
and is not clear on how that is a community benefit as a whole.

CHAIR MEDAWAR asked if this is a project that the commissioners would like to see go forward.
COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN stated that this project has a lot of good amenities and
suggested that the Planning Commission look at the qualitative value. If the 50% bonus is justified,
then the project can be recommended to the City Council.

A brief discussion ensued.

COMMISSIONER YOO made a motion, seconded by COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN to,

  OPEN THE PUBLIC HEARING

There being no objection, CHAIR MEDAWAR so ordered.

Ryan Ash, Vice President of Development, Vestar stated that they are owners of the Peninsula
Center and partners with the City for the past eleven years. He stated that he began working on
this project with city staff for the past six years when the general plan was being updated. Mr. Ash
stated that as it stands the community benefit is 73% to the value they receive according to the
third-party appraisal that Vestar paid for, but worked directly with the City. He stated that if there
were a value of zero dollars for the parking or the public plaza, their project still qualifies under
the City’s density bonus program. Mr. Ash explained that there will be an excess of private parking
stalls and it would be in his interest to charge for the extra parking stalls and stated that residents
will not be allowed to park in the 85 public parking stalls. He added that this will be outlined in the
parking management agreement and there will be security monitoring to make sure that it is only
used for public parking.

COMMISSIONER NICKLAS asked if community benefit is over 70% of the benefit received by
Vestar including the 30 additional units. Mr. Ash clarified the calculation for the density bonus,
which results in a 50% bonus equal to twenty-one units. Mr. Ash stated that the nine units would
not be built unless there was an incentive tied to them and added that using the State Density
Law, they could get to 90-units and would not need to provide community benefits.

In response to a question by COMMISSIONER SCHACHTER, Mr. Ash stated that Vestar values
its membership with the community. He stated that his partner Jeff Axtell has lived in the
community for sixty years. He stated that they have been great community members and have
provided parking stalls to the PVP Performing Arts Center when they are needed.

COMMISSIONER SCHACHTER stated that this is not personal, but the concern is with other
projects that will be considered in the future.

 COMMISSIONER YOO asked if the affordable units would be enough to qualify for the City’s
density bonus. Mr. Ash stated that the statement is accurate.

COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN stated that the State density bonus law is different than
what is being proposed. First the State density program is for sale properties not rentals. She
stated that the proposed affordable housing is 15%, which would only award about a 10% density
bonus. She argued that what the City is considering because of the combination of amenities
versus only providing affordable housing would only get them about a 10% density bonus.

Mr. Ash stated that he is happy with the project they are proposing and stated that he feels they
have balanced it well between the benefit to the developer and the benefit to the City. He stated
that he believes this will be an excellent amenity in partnership with the community going forward.

COMMISSIONER YOO asked for clarification on how the affordable units will qualify him for the
density bonus and asked why the valuation is not higher. Mr. Ash stated that the appraisal was a
direct calculation of what can be charged for the affordable units based on the average median
income in the area.

COMMISSIONER YOO asked about the process to qualify for one of the affordable housing units.
Director Naughton stated that City will be preparing an affordable housing monitoring program.
She stated that the applicants will need to be income qualified. The developer will select their
tenants and will need to provide documentation to show that the tenants in the affordable housing
units are income-qualified and the City will confirm this.

Director Naughton stated that this will be the first rental project in the City and diversifying the
housing stock in the City is important. Also, there is currently no incentive for moderate rental in
the State density bonus law so it would be difficult to see moderate rental housing as part of a
project. She stated that staff see this as a positive contribution to the City.

In response to a question by COMMISSIONER YOO, Director Naughton stated that the State has
rent control provisions, however, the City has not adopted nor are there any plans to adopt rental
control in the City.

VICE CHAIR OLSON stated that he believes this is a great project.

Brendan Kearns, Resident, stated that he grew up on the hill and moved back a few years ago
and saw the notice for this project and was delighted. Mr. Kearns stated that he has lived in
various cities that have walkability, the dynamism of people on the streets, and there was mixed-
use and is thrilled about a project like this in an area that has underutilized space. Mr. Kearns
added that he is pleased with how the commission has interrogated this project applicant for
benefit of the community. Mr. Kearns voiced his support for longer affordable housing terms or
more affordable units rather than any parking arrangement.

COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN stated that according to the State’s density bonus law, the
developer would need to provide 24% of the units at low income to qualify for a 50% density bonus
and there would be no discretion on the design. She stated that she respects that the developer
is proposing a project that has nice architectural details and fits in well with the community,
however this is a for-profit developer trying to utilize the system in a way to get more of an
advantage than what they are giving. She stated that she feels that the job of the Planning

COMMISSIONER REPP-LOADSMAN stated that she still has concerns that the City is giving a

qualify the project for the 50% density bonus. Mr. Ash stated that with the affordable housing
proposed, the project would qualify, as it would be at 27% of what is required as defined in the

 density bonus program. Director Naughton stated that it is still a discretionary decision of the City
